result.unit: ch2 other side of the Earth, part 2 (4:30-5:57)
result.summary:
Range 270–357.66 (end of s034 through s044) was checked against the narration words, all 30 marker cues and the visual plans. I used the 1 fps sheets, a 4 fps motion and flash scan, and about 45 full-size frames saved in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/review/w2/w3_ch2b/x/.

What works:
- No marker event is more than 0.5 s late.
- There are no black or empty frames and no 1-frame flashes.
- The longest low-motion stretch is 2 s (315.5–317.5).
- These beats all land: Argentina→China with the Kenney mini, the 1-in-8 antipode map, the waffle card (29 vs 13), the hemisphere-cap search and flood, the 2x3 X-stamp grid, the 89% flip, the callback montage, and the 1875 / JUICE CHECK / SUBSCRIBE close.

The weak spot is the chapter's climax, the Pacific pour (s041):
- Africa's flying polygon wraps the horizon and paints the whole globe solid orange for about 0.6 s (blocker).
- The finished pour fills the entire visible Pacific, so "with room to spare" and the Explorer "waving from the leftover blue" never read. His end point is itself a filled cell.

A thin dashed line also appears along the 180° meridian (the date line) on every overlay globe facing the Pacific (water half, pour, montage tile). It comes from a mipmap seam in the engine's lib/globe.js and has a one-line fix.

Two more framing problems:
- The 1875 pyramid's 4th corner never enters the frame, so only 3 of the 4 corner flares show.
- The drip globe's South Pole '?' sits in the bottom 12%.

There are also two small polish items.

issues.problem: Right on 'every continent on Earth,' the whole globe flashes solid orange for about 0.6 s. Stray white polygon edges race around the edge of the globe, and at 323.7 black triangular wedges cut into the bottom. Cause: Africa's flying shape (t0 = drop+1.3, drawn from t0-0.25 = 323.11) starts on the far side and encloses the point directly opposite the camera (about 8N 22E). L.globePath(pj, arrs, true) pins its hidden vertices to the visible edge, so the outline wraps the whole horizon and both the shadow and orange fills cover the entire globe.
issues.evidence: x/f_323.3.jpg and x/f_323.6.jpg: entire globe orange with white lines along the edge. x/f_323.7.jpg: full orange plus black wedges at the bottom. x/f_323.2.jpg: whole globe tinted (alpha ramping in). x/f_323.15.jpg and x/f_323.8.jpg / x/f_324.0.jpg are normal. All under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/review/w2/w3_ch2b/.
issues.fix: ch2.js, section 's041 U', draw2d drop loop. Right after `const R = L.rotAB(d.c, pac, k);` add `const cc = L.rotVec(d.c, R); if (!pj.xyz(cc[0], cc[1], cc[2], false)[2]) continue;` so a continent is never filled or shadowed while its centre is still behind the globe. Africa then appears as it crosses the visible edge at about 324.0 and still lands at 324.46. Optional: ramp alpha over 0.15 s from that moment.

issues.problem: A thin dashed line runs pole to pole along the 180° meridian (the date line) on every overlay globe facing the Pacific.
